{{Short description|Topological construction defined up to homotopy}}
In [[mathematics]], especially [[homotopy theory]], the '''homotopy fiber''' (sometimes called the '''mapping fiber''')<ref name="rotman">Joseph J. Rotman, ''An Introduction to Algebraic Topology'' (1988) Springer-Verlag {{isbn|0-387-96678-1}} ''(See Chapter 11 for construction.)''</ref>  is part of a construction that associates a [[fibration]] to an arbitrary [[continuous function]] of [[topological spaces]] <math>f:A \to B</math>. It acts as a homotopy theoretic kernel of a mapping of topological spaces due to the fact it yields a long exact sequence of homotopy groups<blockquote><math>\cdots \to \pi_{n+1}(B) \to \pi_n(\text{Hofiber}(f)) \to \pi_n(A) \to \pi_n(B) \to \cdots</math></blockquote>Moreover, the homotopy fiber can be found in other contexts, such as [[homological algebra]], where the distinguished triangle<blockquote><math>C(f)_\bullet[-1] \to A_\bullet \to B_\bullet \xrightarrow{[+1]}</math></blockquote>gives a long exact sequence analogous to the long exact sequence of homotopy groups. There is a [[Duality (mathematics)|dual]] construction called the [[homotopy cofiber]].

== Construction ==
The homotopy fiber has a simple description for a continuous map <math>f:A \to B</math>. If we replace <math>f</math> by a fibration, then the homotopy fiber is simply the fiber of the replacement fibration. We recall this construction of replacing a map by a fibration:

Given such a map, we can replace it with a [[fibration]] by defining the [[mapping path space]] <math>E_f</math> to be the set of pairs <math>(a,\gamma)</math> where <math>a \in A</math> and  <math>\gamma:I \to B</math> (for <math>I = [0,1]</math>) a path such that <math>\gamma(0) = f(a)</math>. We give <math>E_f</math> a topology by giving it the [[subspace topology]] as a subset of <math>A\times B^I</math> (where <math>B^I</math> is the space of paths in <math>B</math> which as a [[function space]] has the [[compact-open topology]]). Then the map <math>E_f \to B</math> given by <math>(a,\gamma) \mapsto \gamma(1)</math> is a fibration. Furthermore, <math>E_f</math> is [[homotopy equivalent]] to <math>A</math> as follows: Embed <math>A</math> as a subspace of <math>E_f</math> by <math>a \mapsto \gamma_a</math> where <math>\gamma_a</math> is the constant path at <math>f(a)</math>. Then <math>E_f</math> [[deformation retract]]s to this subspace by contracting the paths.

The fiber of this fibration (which is only well-defined up to homotopy equivalence) is the '''homotopy fiber'''<blockquote><math>\begin{matrix}
\text{Hofiber}(f) &\to & E_f \\
& & \downarrow \\
& & B
\end{matrix}</math></blockquote>which can be defined as the set of all <math>(a,\gamma)</math> with <math>a \in A</math> and <math>\gamma:I \to B</math> a path such that <math>\gamma(0) = f(a)</math> and <math>\gamma(1) = *</math> for some fixed basepoint <math>* \in B</math>. A consequence of this definition is that if two points of <math>B</math> are in the same path connected component, then their homotopy fibers are homotopy equivalent.

=== As a homotopy limit ===
Another way to construct the homotopy fiber of a map is to consider the [[Homotopy colimit|homotopy limit]]'''<ref name=":1">{{Cite web|last=Dugger|first=Daniel|date=|title=A Primer on Homotopy Colimits|url=https://pages.uoregon.edu/ddugger/hocolim.pdf|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201203225718/https://pages.uoregon.edu/ddugger/hocolim.pdf|archive-date=3 Dec 2020|access-date=|website=}}</ref>'''<sup>pg 21</sup> of the diagram<blockquote><math>\underset{\leftarrow}{\text{holim}}\left(\begin{matrix}
& & * \\
& & \downarrow \\
A & \xrightarrow{f} & B
\end{matrix}\right)
\simeq F_f</math></blockquote>this is because computing the homotopy limit amounts to finding the pullback of the diagram<blockquote><math>\begin{matrix}
& & B^I \\
& & \downarrow \\
A \times * & \xrightarrow{f} & B\times B
\end{matrix}</math></blockquote>where the vertical map is the source and target map of a path <math>\gamma: I \to B</math>, so<blockquote><math>\gamma \mapsto (\gamma(0), \gamma(1))</math></blockquote>This means the homotopy limit is in the collection of maps<blockquote><math>\left\{(a, \gamma) \in A \times B^I : f(a) = \gamma(0) \text{ and } \gamma(1) = *\right\}</math></blockquote>which is exactly the homotopy fiber as defined above.

If <math>x_0</math> and <math>x_1</math> can be connected by a path <math>\delta</math> in <math>B</math>, then the diagrams 

<blockquote><math>\begin{matrix}
& & x_0 \\
& & \downarrow \\
A & \xrightarrow{f} & B
\end{matrix}</math></blockquote> and <blockquote><math>\begin{matrix}
& & x_1 \\
& & \downarrow \\
A & \xrightarrow{f} & B
\end{matrix}</math></blockquote> are homotopy equivalent to the diagram <blockquote><math>\begin{matrix}
& & [0,1] \\
& & \downarrow{\delta} \\
A & \xrightarrow{f} & B
\end{matrix}</math></blockquote> and thus the homotopy fibers of <math>x_0</math> and <math>x_1</math> are isomorphic in <math>\text{hoTop}</math>. Therefore we often speak about the homotopy fiber of a map without specifying a base point.

== Properties ==

=== Homotopy fiber of a fibration ===
In the special case that the original map <math>f</math> was a fibration with fiber <math>F</math>, then the homotopy equivalence <math>A \to E_f</math> given above will be a map of fibrations over <math>B</math>.  This will induce a [[morphism]] of their [[long exact sequence]]s of [[homotopy group]]s, from which (by applying the [[Five Lemma]], as is done in the [[Puppe sequence]]) one can see that the map {{math|''F'' → ''F''<sub>''f''</sub>}} is  a [[weak equivalence (homotopy theory)|weak equivalence]].  Thus the above given construction reproduces the same homotopy type if there already is one.

=== Duality with mapping cone ===
The homotopy fiber is dual to the [[mapping cone (topology)|mapping cone]], much as the [[mapping path space]] is dual to the [[mapping cylinder]].<ref name="may">[[J.P. May]], ''[http://www.math.uchicago.edu/~may/CONCISE/ConciseRevised.pdf A Concise Course in Algebraic Topology]'', (1999) Chicago Lectures in Mathematics {{isbn|0-226-51183-9}} ''(See chapters 6,7.)''</ref>

== Examples ==

=== Loop space ===
Given a topological space <math>X</math> and the inclusion of a point<blockquote><math>\iota: \{x_0\} \hookrightarrow X</math></blockquote>the homotopy fiber of this map is then<blockquote><math>\left\{(x_0, \gamma) \in \{x_0\} \times X^I : x_0 = \gamma(0) \text{ and } \gamma(1) = x_0\right\}</math></blockquote>which is the loop space <math>\Omega X</math>.

See also: [[Path space fibration]].

=== From a covering space ===
Given a universal covering<blockquote><math>\pi:\tilde{X} \to X</math></blockquote>the homotopy fiber <math>\text{Hofiber}(\pi)</math> has the property<blockquote><math>\pi_{k}(\text{Hofiber}(\pi)) = \begin{cases}
\pi_1(X) & k = 0  \\
0 & k \geq 1
\end{cases}</math></blockquote>which can be seen by looking at the long exact sequence of the homotopy groups for the fibration. This is analyzed further below by looking at the Whitehead tower.

== Applications ==

=== Postnikov tower ===
One main application of the homotopy fiber is in the construction of the [[Postnikov tower]]. For a (nice enough) topological space <math>X</math>, we can construct a sequence of spaces <math>\left\{X_n\right\}_{n \geq 0}</math> and maps <math>f_n: X_n \to X_{n-1}</math> where<blockquote><math>\pi_k\left(X_n\right) = \begin{cases}
  \pi_k(X) & k \leq n \\
         0 & \text{ otherwise }
\end{cases}</math></blockquote>and<blockquote><math>X \simeq \underset{\leftarrow}{\text{lim}}\left(X_k\right)</math></blockquote>Now, these maps <math>f_n</math> ''can be iteratively constructed using homotopy fibers''. This is because we can take a map<blockquote><math>X_{n-1} \to K\left(\pi_n(X), n - 1\right)</math></blockquote>representing a cohomology class in<blockquote><math>H^{n-1}\left(X_{n-1}, \pi_n(X)\right)</math></blockquote>and construct the homotopy fiber<blockquote><math>\underset{\leftarrow}{\text{holim}}\left(\begin{matrix}
                           && * \\
                           && \downarrow \\
  X_{n-1} & \xrightarrow{f} & K\left(\pi_n(X), n - 1\right)
\end{matrix}\right)
\simeq X_n</math></blockquote>In addition, notice the homotopy fiber of <math>f_n: X_n \to X_{n-1}</math> is<blockquote><math>\text{Hofiber}\left(f_n\right) \simeq K\left(\pi_n(X), n\right)</math></blockquote>showing the homotopy fiber acts like a homotopy-theoretic kernel. Note this fact can be shown by looking at the long exact sequence for the fibration constructing the homotopy fiber.

=== Maps from the Whitehead tower ===
The dual notion of the Postnikov tower is the [[Whitehead tower]] which gives a sequence of spaces <math>\{X^n\}_{n \geq 0}</math> and maps <math>f^n: X^n \to X^{n-1}</math> where<blockquote><math>\pi_k\left(X^n\right) = \begin{cases}
\pi_k(X) & k \geq n \\
0 & \text{otherwise}
\end{cases}</math></blockquote>hence <math>X^0 \simeq X</math>. If we take the induced map<blockquote><math>f^{n+1}_0: X^{n+1} \to X</math></blockquote>the homotopy fiber of this map recovers the <math>n</math>-th postnikov approximation <math>X_n</math> since the long exact sequence of the fibration<blockquote><math>\begin{matrix}
  \text{Hofiber}\left(f^{n+1}_0\right) & \to & X^{n+1} \\
                                            && \downarrow \\
                                            && X
\end{matrix}</math></blockquote>we get<blockquote><math>\begin{matrix}
  \to & \pi_{k+1}\left(\text{Hofiber}\left(f^{n+1}_0\right)\right) & \to & \pi_{k+1}(X^{n+1})            & \to & \pi_{k+1}(X) & \to \\
      & \pi_{k}\left(\text{Hofiber}\left(f^{n+1}_0\right)\right)   & \to & \pi_{k}\left(X^{n+1}\right)   & \to & \pi_{k}(X)   & \to \\
      & \pi_{k-1}\left(\text{Hofiber}\left(f^{n+1}_0\right)\right) & \to & \pi_{k-1}\left(X^{n+1}\right) & \to & \pi_{k-1}(X) & \to
\end{matrix}</math></blockquote>which gives isomorphisms<blockquote><math>\pi_{k-1}\left(\text{Hofiber}\left(f^{n+1}_0\right)\right) \cong \pi_k(X)</math></blockquote>for <math>k \leq n</math>.
